Verdict

Reviewed 27 Oct 2026 · next 25 Jan 2027

Browser-first sanitizer and the de facto standard. It parses untrusted HTML with the same DOM the browser will use, which is why it holds up against mutation XSS. One dependency, 11.7 KB gzip, 45M weekly downloads, and zero executions in our 25-vector browser harness. The gap is release integrity: npm publishes are manual and the tarball is unattested, although the release artifacts are SLSA-attested and Sigstore-signed and the shipped dist files match those hashes.

Current Reviewed version 3.4.17 Requirement: Sanitize untrusted HTML before rendering

Reasoning

  1. 0 of 25 XSS vectors executed after DOMPurify, while the unsanitized control executed 11.
  2. 3.4.17 is clean in OSV. Its 33 historical advisories are all fixed, including a CRITICAL SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES bypass fixed in 3.4.17 on 2026-10-22.
  3. Security engineering is unusually strong: fuzz, CodeQL, dependency-review and OpenSSF Scorecard workflows, plus SLSA provenance and Sigstore signatures on GitHub release artifacts.
  4. The release artifacts are verifiable even though npm is not: the 3.4.17 SLSA subject hashes match the four dist files shipped in the npm tarball byte-for-byte, so the shipped code can be tied back to the attested build.
  5. Parsing with a real DOM matches the eventual render context, which is the main defence against mXSS.
  6. One runtime dependency (@types/trusted-types), 1.65 MB install and 11.7 KB gzip.
  7. It strips handlers and javascript: URLs, removes iframe/style, and keeps allowed markup such as img and svg.

Caveats

  • npm publishes are manual and unattested; provenance exists only on GitHub release artifacts. Verification is possible by hashing the dist files against the release attestation, but it does not happen automatically on install.
  • The advisory rate is high: 33 advisories, roughly half of them in 2026. Staying current is not optional, and 3.4.17 specifically fixes two CVEs from 22 Oct 2026.
  • Dual-licensed MPL-2.0 or Apache-2.0; select Apache-2.0 in your policy.
  • Needs a DOM. In Node you must supply jsdom/happy-dom yourself or use isomorphic-dompurify, which is far heavier.
  • The default configuration is permissive by design: it allows images, links and SVG. Tighten ALLOWED_TAGS/ALLOWED_ATTR for model output.

Decision context

Approved

dompurify is the primary choice for Sanitize untrusted HTML before rendering. This package is classified as Adopted.

Use DOMPurify wherever a browser DOM is available, because parsing with the real DOM is the strongest defence against mutation XSS. Use sanitize-html for Node and SSR, where jsdom would add 27 MB for the same outcome. Use rehype-sanitize when content already flows through remark/rehype, which is the case for the assistant-ui react-markdown pipeline. Keep isomorphic-dompurify on hold: it is correct, but only worth its jsdom footprint if you need DOMPurify specifically on the server. Keep xss on hold: it is fast and safe in the harness, but its escape-not-strip model and lack of independent advisory coverage make it a weaker default. insane and sanitizer are abandoned and must not be used. No package in this category publishes npm provenance, so pin exact versions, subscribe to advisories for the chosen sanitizer, and re-review every 90 days. A 25-vector headless-Chrome corpus executed 11 vectors unsanitized and zero after every tested sanitizer.
